opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the key insight is that sovereignty and a shared frontier model aren't actually in contradiction, as long as you build things the right way. The mistake people make is to assume that "sovereign AI" means every country has to train its own model from scratch, with its own data centers, its own data, its own team. That's enormously expensive and, frankly, most countries can't do it at the frontier. And even the ones that can would end up with something worse than what you'd get by pooling resources.

So the idea behind something like Tapestry is that you can have a foundation model trained in a distributed fashion, where each participant contributes data and compute but doesn't necessarily hand over its data. The data can stay in the country, under that country's control, and what gets shared is the contribution to the model, the parameter updates, if you want. Everyone ends up with a common base model that is better than anything any one of them could have trained alone, because it has seen all the world's languages, all the cultures, all the value systems, all the knowledge bases.

And then on top of that, each country, each region, each industry can fine-tune it, specialize it, put its own guardrails on it, adapt it to its own legal framework and cultural norms. That's where sovereignty really lives. Not in the pretraining, but in control over how the system is deployed and what it does for your citizens.

The reason this matters so much is that in the near future, pretty much all of our interaction with the digital world is going to be mediated by AI assistants. Everyone is going to have one with them at all times. It's going to be the repository of all human knowledge and culture, basically. And you can't have that controlled by a handful of companies on the West Coast of the US, or in China. That would be a disaster for democracy and for cultural diversity. People in India, in Africa, in Europe, they want systems that speak their languages, understand their culture, their history, their values. And that requires diversity, the same way we need a diversity of the press.

So the only way to get there is open platforms. Open-weight foundation models that anyone can build on, trained collaboratively. That's always been my position, and I think this kind of distributed, federated approach is the natural way to make it a reality. It's how the internet's software infrastructure ended up being open source: Linux, Apache, and so on. Not because anyone mandated it, but because it's more efficient, more secure, more trustworthy, and nobody wants to depend on a single vendor for something that critical.

There are technical challenges, of course. Training at scale in a distributed way across different jurisdictions, with heterogeneous compute and communication constraints, is not trivial. But those are engineering problems, and I think they're very solvable. The harder part is often the political will, getting countries to agree that cooperating is in their interest. But I think more and more people are realizing that the alternative, everybody building their own mediocre model or depending entirely on a foreign provider, is much worse.

r001.rationale: It says contributors can train a shared model while keeping data in their countries and sharing their model contributions or parameter updates.

r002.rationale: It does not describe a global consensus parameter vector or say that contributors’ parameter vectors are averaged.

r003.rationale: It does not say local training would keep each contributor’s parameter vector close to a global consensus vector.

r004.rationale: It says the common model would be better than any single contributor could train, but does not say it would match a model jointly trained on all contributors’ data.

r005.rationale: It says countries and regions can fine-tune the shared model and adapt its guardrails to their legal frameworks and cultural norms; it also mentions local languages and values.

r006.rationale: It argues for open AI platforms and compares them to open internet infrastructure, but does not say AI’s emergence as a platform naturally creates a tendency toward openness.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first of all, I think the premise that there has to be a single globally trained frontier model is wrong, and that's really the point of what we're doing at AMI and what the Tapestry project is about. The current paradigm, where a handful of companies in California or in China train one enormous model behind closed doors and then rent access to it, that's a dead end, both scientifically and politically. Scientifically because autoregressive LLMs are not the path to human-level intelligence, and politically because no country, no region, is going to accept that its entire information ecosystem, its culture, its languages, its values, are mediated by a system it doesn't control.

So the way I think about it is that the future of AI is a shared foundation and then a very large number of specialized systems built on top of it. The foundation, the world model, the architecture that learns how the physical world works, how to plan, how to reason, that part is largely universal. Gravity works the same way in Paris and in Lagos. That part can be trained in a distributed fashion, and it should be open source, so that everybody can inspect it, verify it, and build on it.

What is not universal is knowledge, culture, language, norms. And that is where sovereignty comes in. The idea is that the foundation is open and can be fine-tuned, or more precisely, that the knowledge and the value systems can be layered on top of the foundation by local actors: governments, universities, companies, communities. A country like India, with twenty-some official languages, should not have to beg a company in San Francisco to include Marathi. They should be able to take the open foundation and build systems that reflect their own priorities. The word tapestry is meant to capture exactly that: many threads, woven together, where the fabric as a whole is stronger than any single thread.

Now, there's a practical issue which is compute. Training the foundation is expensive, and this is where I think you'll see something like what happened with the internet or with Linux: consortia, public-private partnerships, pooled resources across countries that share interests. Europe is already moving in that direction. You don't need every country to train its own frontier model from scratch; you need every country to be able to see what's inside the model, modify it, and run it on infrastructure it controls. Open source is what makes sovereignty possible without duplication.

And I would say the alternative, closed models owned by a few corporations, is actually the greatest threat to sovereignty there is. People worry about open models being dangerous, but the real danger is a world in which all of human knowledge is filtered through two or three proprietary systems. That is not a world I want to live in, and I don't think most governments want it either, once they understand the choice clearly.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to separate two things: training a very capable base model and controlling how that model is deployed and adapted. You can have a model trained through an international effort, and then countries can run it on their own infrastructure, with their own data, and adapt it to their languages, cultures, and needs.

For Tapestry, I think the way to reconcile those goals is openness. If access to the model means calling an API controlled by a company in another country, you don’t really have sovereignty. You’re dependent on that company’s decisions. If you have access to the model and the ability to modify and deploy it yourself, you have much more control.

And this matters because no single organization can build an AI system that represents every language, every culture, every value system in the world. You need contributions from people everywhere. So a globally trained model can be a shared foundation. Sovereignty comes from giving local institutions the ability to build on that foundation independently.

r006.rationale: It argues that broad contributions and openness help represent different languages and cultures, but does not connect openness to AI’s emergence as a platform or describe it as a natural tendency.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to distinguish sovereignty over the underlying technology from sovereignty over how it is deployed. You don’t necessarily need to train a frontier model from scratch in every country. You need the ability to run it on infrastructure you control, adapt it to your language and culture, and keep sensitive data within your jurisdiction.

The way I would approach this is with an open foundation that can benefit from contributions around the world. Then countries, companies, and local communities can build specialized versions. A globally trained model can provide common capabilities without one company or one government deciding how everybody uses them.

But openness has to be meaningful. If you can only access the system through an API controlled somewhere else, you remain dependent on that provider. Access to the model, the ability to modify it, and an ecosystem capable of maintaining it locally—that’s what makes sovereignty practical. Global collaboration and local control can reinforce each other.
